source.title: Applying Sport Scientist Roles Within Organizations

paper.citation: Gleason, B. H., Suchomel, T. J., Brewer, C., McMahon, E., Lis, R. P., & Stone, M. H. (2023). Applying sport scientist roles within organizations. Strength & Conditioning Journal. https://doi.org/10.1519/SSC.0000000000000810
paper.abstract: How can sport organizations structure, resource, and integrate sport-scientist roles, and what common implementation problems should leaders avoid? Participants: No recruited sample. Setting: Primarily US professional, collegiate, and sport-system organizations, with selected international models. Roles considered: Part-time and full-time practitioners, researchers, program managers, managers, faculty partnerships, integrated support teams, and high-performance managers. Inclusion and exclusion boundaries: Narrative organizational guidance rather than a systematic review, workforce survey, or comparative evaluation. Design: Narrative applied review and conceptual framework. Evidence base: Prior literature, organizational examples, and the authors' professional experience. Comparator: Conceptual comparison of role structures, from individual part-time appointments through integrated academic-athletic models and full-time leadership. Measurements and outcomes: No predefined search strategy, quality appraisal, organizational outcome measure, or quantitative synthesis is reported. Analysis: Descriptive mapping of role responsibilities, benefits, constraints, and proposed best practices.
paper.tldr: This applied organizational article maps sport-scientist role configurations, high-performance management responsibilities, and failure modes relevant to building sustainable sport-science operations in US sport. The authors classify sport-scientist work broadly as practitioner, researcher, program manager, or manager, with roles often blended according to budget, workflow, access, and organizational need. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Design: Narrative applied review and conceptual framework. Evidence base: Prior literature, organizational examples, and the authors' professional experience. Comparator: Conceptual comparison of role structures, from individual part-time appointments through integrated academic-athletic models and full-time leadership. Measurements and outcomes: No predefined search strategy, quality appraisal, organizational outcome measure, or quantitative synthesis is reported. Analysis: Descriptive mapping of role responsibilities, benefits, constraints, and proposed best practices.
paper.findings: The authors classify sport-scientist work broadly as practitioner, researcher, program manager, or manager, with roles often blended according to budget, workflow, access, and organizational need. Assigning sport-science duties to an already full-time strength coach can create skill mismatch, excessive workload, communication problems, and service-delivery risk. The high-performance manager is framed as a performance facilitator, relationship builder, strategic thinker, and quality-control manager; the authors recommend separating that leadership role from routine practitioner duties. The authors favor defining needs and roles before buying technology, maintaining stable data processes over multiple years, and taking a people-first approach to integration. Their concluding sequence is to identify contextual needs and goals, construct and fund roles clearly, and then initiate integration.
paper.limitations: Recommendations are not estimates of effectiveness; the article does not compare organizational structures against athlete, staff, financial, or decision-quality outcomes. The authors describe some claims as observations or personal experience, and no formal evidence-selection process is reported. US funding, governance, employment, and academic-athletic conditions may not transfer to other sport systems or institutions. Proposed structures vary greatly in cost, authority, access, stability, and political feasibility; titles alone do not confer competence or integration. The authors acknowledge that integrated support is not currently feasible for every organization and call for further work on sustainable best practices.
paper.practicalImplications: Start with the decisions and services the organization must support, then define authority, competence, workload, data stewardship, and success criteria. Protect leadership bandwidth, use technology only after people and processes are specified, and judge the operating model by decision quality, continuity, staff coordination, and athlete service rather than by visible tools or job titles.
